subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find all common tangents to the circles x² + y² − 2x − 6y + 6 = 0 and x² + y² = 1.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, SENIOR INTER MATHS-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.21 — LAQ chapter 1 Circle, answer 8. No appearance tag is printed beside this answer. The mark split is OURS, not the book’s: this answer sits on a two-column page with no printed margin tags. It is patterned on the nearest printed split of the same shape in this chapter — book p.16, answer 3, which prints 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 for the same two-equations-then-centre-then-circle shape, and book p.17, answer 4, which prints 1 + 1 + 1 + 4. Star rank: the book gives the CIRCLE LAQ chapter ★★★ in its LAQ chapter table (book p.13), in the chapter header (book p.14) and in the LAQ hit list header (book p.7), so every Circle LAQ entry takes stars 3. That rank belongs to the CHAPTER, not to this question. Paper position: Maths-2B Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Circle holds Q18 and Q19. An LAQ on this paper is 7 marks, never 8 — the 2026-27 move to 8-mark long answers is first year only. Every number was re-derived and the book is correct: I = (1/3, 1), E = (−1, −3), the transverse pair is 4y² + 3xy − 3x − 9y + 5 = 0 and the direct pair is 4x² − 3xy − x − 3y − 5 = 0. FIGURE SCOPE: the question does not say "draw", so the diagram step carries NO marks; the figure is included because the answer needs BOTH centres of similitude and their positions are the argument. insider_note: "All common tangents" means four lines, given here as two pair equations — one pair through I and one through E. Answering with only one pair loses half the marks even if that pair is perfect.

steps.label: Centres and radii
steps.margin_note: One mark. The second circle is already in centre-radius form, so read it directly.
steps.memory_tip: x² + y² = 1 is the unit circle: centre at the origin, radius 1.
steps.why: One circle is given in general form and the other in the simplest possible form. Reading both to the same centre-and-radius pair is what makes them comparable.
common_mistakes: Treating x² + y² = 1 as having radius 1 squared, so r₂ = 1 is written as r₂² = 1 and then used as a radius.

steps.label: Compare C₁C₂ with r₁ + r₂
steps.margin_note: One mark. Four common tangents exist only when C₁C₂ > r₁ + r₂; say so before finding any of them.
steps.memory_tip: Circles fully apart give four common tangents: two direct and two transverse.
lines: ∴ Each circle lies entirely outside the other,
so there are four common tangents.
steps.why: Comparing √10 with 3 is the same as comparing 10 with 9, so no decimals are needed. Only when the circles are fully apart do both a direct pair and a transverse pair exist.
common_mistakes: Comparing √10 with 3 by rounding and getting them equal.
Claiming two tangents instead of four.

steps.label: Both centres of similitude
steps.margin_note: One mark. Both points are needed: I gives the transverse pair, E gives the direct pair.
steps.memory_tip: Internal division gives I and transverse tangents; external division gives E and direct tangents.
steps.why: Each pair of common tangents passes through one point. The transverse pair meets at I between the circles; the direct pair meets at E outside them. Both are section-formula points on the line of centres.
common_mistakes: Finding only one of the two points.

steps.label: Pair of transverse common tangents
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Use the simpler circle x² + y² − 1 = 0 for S here; the tangents are common, so either circle gives the same pair.
steps.memory_tip: S₁₁ · S = S₁², with S the simple circle x² + y² − 1 = 0.
lines: From I(1/3, 1) to S ≡ x² + y² − 1 = 0:
steps.why: The tangents are common to both circles, so the pair may be built from whichever circle gives lighter algebra — here the unit circle. Both sides carry a ninth, which cancels, and the x² terms cancel as well.
common_mistakes: Using the first circle for S and the unit circle for S₁₁.

steps.label: Pair of direct common tangents
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Same formula, different point: E instead of I.
steps.memory_tip: Repeat the previous step with E(−1, −3). Only the point changes.
lines: From E(−1, −3) to S ≡ x² + y² − 1 = 0:
steps.why: The two pair equations together are the four common tangents. Squaring S₁ removes the sign, so (−x − 3y − 1)² is the same as (x + 3y + 1)², which is why the working looks slightly different from the transverse case.
common_mistakes: Keeping the minus signs inside the square and dropping a cross term.
Forgetting to divide the final equation by 2.

steps.label: The picture
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own; the question does not ask for a diagram. Marking I and E in rough is enough to keep the two pairs apart.
steps.memory_tip: I sits between the circles; E sits outside both, past the smaller one.

elements.text: I is inside, E is outside both circles

steps.why: The two centres of similitude are on the same straight line through C₁ and C₂ but on opposite sides of the picture. Marking them makes it obvious which pair of tangents is being built at each stage.
common_mistakes: Placing E between the circles, where I belongs.
Drawing the circles overlapping, which removes the transverse pair.
